1.DevOps: 
DevOps is a software development approach in which development and operations teams 
collaborate throughout the entire lifecycle of a system, from design and development to 
deployment and maintenance. 
The term DevOps is derived from: 
 Development (Dev) 
 Operations (Ops) 
踰踱踲踳 It combines processes, tools, and culture to enable faster and reliable software delivery. 
꾄 Need for DevOps (Why DevOps?) 
Traditionally: 
 Developers aim for frequent changes 
 Operations aim for system stability 
 Testers aim for risk reduction 
This leads to conﬂicts and delays. 
踰踱踲踳 DevOps solves this by: 
 Improving communication and collaboration 
 Enabling automation 
 Ensuring

Ops solves this by: 
 Improving communication and collaboration 
 Enabling automation 
 Ensuring continuous delivery 
 Availability of cloud infrastructure 
꾄 Goals of DevOps 
 Fast delivery of software 
 Reduced failure rate 
 Shorter lead time between ﬁxes 
 Faster recovery (MTTR) 
 Automation of processes 
 Reduced operational cost 
 Standardized environments 
 Improved eƯiciency and proﬁt

 Faster bug ﬁxing

 Increased productivity 
 Better employee engagement 
꾆 Business Beneﬁts 
 Faster product delivery 
 Stable environment 
 Improved customer satisfaction 
 More innovation time 
Phases of DevOps Architecture 
DevOps architecture consists of the following stages: 
1. Plan 
 Requirements are gathered and analyzed 
 Project scope, cost, and schedule are deﬁned 
 Tools: Jira 
2. Code 
 Developers write the code based on requirements 
 Project is divided into smaller modules 
 Version control is maintained 
 Tools: Git 
3. Build 
 Source code is compiled into executable form 
 All modules are integrated 
 Tools: Maven, Gradle

4. Test 
 Software is tested to detect bugs

 Tools: Selenium, JUnit, PyTest 
5. Integrate 
 New code is integrated with existing code 
 Ensures smooth functioning of system

6. Deploy

 Detects issues like server failure, low memory, etc. 
 Tools: Nagios, ELK Stack

2.Version Control System – Git and GitHub : 
A Version Control System (VCS) is software that helps developers track changes, 
collaborate, and maintain the history of source code. 
Functions: 
 Allows multiple developers to work simultaneously 
 Prevents overwriting of changes 
 Maintains complete version history 
膆 2. Types of Version Control Systems : 
꾆 1. Local Version Control System (LVCS) 
Deﬁnition: 
Stores ﬁles and versions only on a local system. 
Example: 
 RCS (Revision Control System) 
Advantages: 
 Simple to use

 Fast 
Disadvantages: 
 No collaboration 
 High risk of data loss 
 2. Centralized Version Control System (CVCS) 
 Uses a central server to store ﬁles 
 Example: SVN 
Advantages: 
 Easy to manage 
 Centralized control 
Disadvantages: 
 Single point of failure 
 Requires internet 
꾆 3. Distributed Version Control System (DVCS) 
 Each user has a complete copy of repository 
 Example: Git 
Advantages: 
 Works oƯline 
 Faster operations 
 Backup available 
Disadvantages: 
 Complex for beginners 
膆 3. Git 
Git is a distributed version control system developed by Linus Torvalds in 2005 for Linux 
kernel development. 
꾆 Features of Git: 
 Free and open-source 
 Tracks all changes

꾆 Features of Git: 
 Free and open-source 
 Tracks all changes (add, modify, delete) 
 Fast and scalable 
 Supports branching and merging 
 Works in distributed environment 
 Secure using SHA-1 hashing 
꾆 Git Workﬂow: 
1. Working Directory → Modify ﬁles 
2. Staging Area (git add) → Prepare ﬁles 
3. Repository (git commit) → Save version 
✔ Files Types: 
 Untracked ﬁles – Not added 
 Tracked ﬁles – Added and monitored

꾆 Basic Git Commands: 
 git init → Create repository 
 git add → Add ﬁles to staging 
 git status → Check status 
 git commit -m → Save changes 
 git log → View history 
꾆 Branching in Git: 
 Used to create separate development paths 
 Commands: 
o git branch → Create branch 
o git checkout → Switch branch 
o git merge → Merge branches

 Repository: Storage of project 
 Working Directory: Where editing happens 
 Staging Area: Temporary storage before commit 
 Commit: Snapshot of changes 
 Clone: Copy repository 
 Pull: Get updates 
 Push: Send updates 
 HEAD: Points to latest commit 
 Blob, Tree: Internal storage

Get updates

꾆 Disadvantages of Git: 
 Learning curve for beginners 
 Merge conﬂicts

膆 5. GitHub (Web-Based Platform) 
GitHub is a web-based hosting service for Git repositories that enables collaboration and 
project management. 
꾆 Features of GitHub: 
 Code hosting 
 Collaboration 
 Issue & bug tracking

 Pull requests (code review)

꾆 Beneﬁts of GitHub:

膆 6. GitHub Workﬂow (2 Marks) 
踰踱踲踳 Commit → Pull → Push 
 Commit: Save changes locally 
 Pull: Get latest updates from remote 
 Push: Upload changes to GitHub 
膆 7. Remote Operations (Extra Scoring Point) 
 git fetch → Check remote changes 
 git merge → Combine branches 
 git pull → Fetch + merge 
 git push → Upload changes

1.Maven Lifecycle & Project Setup : 
Maven is a build automation and project management tool used to compile, test, 
package, and deploy applications using a predeﬁned lifecycle. 
膆 2. Maven Build Lifecycle 
Maven lifecycle is a sequence of phases that must be followed to build a project. 
꾆 Main Phases: 
1. Validate 
o Checks whether all required information is available 
2. Compile 
o Compiles source code 
3. Test Compile 
o Compiles test code 
4. Test 
o Executes unit tests 
5. Package 
o Packages code into JAR/WAR ﬁle 
6. Install 
o Installs package into local repository 
7. Deploy 
o Deploys package to remote repository 
꾆 Important Note: 
踰踱踲踳

e into local repository 
7. Deploy 
o Deploys package to remote repository 
꾆 Important Note: 
踰踱踲踳 Phases are executed sequentially 
✔ Example: 
If we run: 
mvn package 
It executes: 
validate → compile → test → package 
꾆 Maven Goals: 
 Each phase contains goals (tasks) 
 Example goals: 
o validate 
o compile

o test 
o package 
o install 
o deploy

</project> 
踰踱踲踳 Add dependencies if needed

 Test: 
mvn test 
 Package: 
mvn package 
 Install: 
mvn install

5.POM File in Maven 
Apache Maven 
A POM (Project Object Model) ﬁle is an XML conﬁguration ﬁle (pom.xml) in Maven that 
contains all the information required to build, manage, and conﬁgure a project. 
Purpose of POM File

The POM ﬁle is the heart of a Maven project. It is used to: 
 Deﬁne project structure 
 Manage dependencies 
 Conﬁgure build process 
 Specify plugins and goals 
 Handle project versioning 
Basic Structure of POM File (4–5 Marks) 
Example: 
<project> 
 <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

 <artifactId>demo</artifactId> 
 <version>1.0</version> 
 
 <dependencies> 
 <dependency> 
 <groupId>junit</groupId> 
 <artifactId>junit</artifactId> 
 <version>4.12</version> 
 </dependency> 
 </dependencies> 
</project>

꾆 1. modelVersion 
 Deﬁnes POM model version (usually 4.0.0) 
꾆 2. groupId 
 Unique ID of organization

2.Jenkins Architecture 
Jenkins is an open-source automation tool that supports Continuous Integration (CI) and 
Continuous Delivery (CD). Its architecture is designed to automate

Continuous Delivery (CD). Its architecture is designed to automate building, testing, and

 Jenkins Workﬂow 
The workﬂow of Jenkins can be summarized as: 
1. Developers commit code changes to the source code repository (e.g., GitHub). 
2. Jenkins continuously monitors the repository for changes. 
3. When changes are detected, Jenkins server triggers a new build. 
4. If the build fails, Jenkins immediately notiﬁes the developers. 
5. If the build succeeds, Jenkins deploys the build to a test server. 
6. The test server runs automated tests and generates feedback. 
7. Jenkins collects feedback and informs developers of

uns automated tests and generates feedback. 
7. Jenkins collects feedback and informs developers of the results. 
8. Once all tests pass, Jenkins deploys the build to the production server.

This process is continuous, ensuring that code is always tested and integrated promptly. 
 
Jenkins Architecture 
Jenkins follows a distributed Master-Slave architecture, which allows it to scale builds 
across multiple machines. Communication between Master and Slaves is via TCP/IP. 
Components: 
a) Jenkins Master 
The Master is the central control unit of Jenkins. Its responsibilities include: 
 Scheduling jobs and builds 
 Assigning jobs to appropriate Slaves 
 Dispatching builds to Slaves for execution 
 Monitoring the status of all Slaves 
 Retrieving build results from Slaves 
 Displaying build and test results on the console 
b) Jenkins Slave (Node/Build Server) 
A Slave is a

isplaying build and test results on the console 
b) Jenkins Slave (Node/Build Server) 
A Slave is a remote machine that executes the jobs assigned by the Master. 
 Slaves can run on any operating system (Windows, Linux, Mac) 
 They perform the actual build, test, and deployment tasks 
 Slaves report results back to the Master

Key Points 
 Jenkins architecture allows distributed builds, improving eƯiciency. 
 Supports continuous monitoring of source code repository. 
 Master-Slave setup provides scalability for large projects. 
 Compatible with multiple operating systems and platforms. 
 Uses plugins to extend functionality for building, testing, and deploying applications.

3. Supports parallel execution on multiple Slaves

DevOps used to automatically build, test, and deploy applications. 
 Eliminates manual work 
 Supports multiple languages (Java, Python, Node.js, etc.) 
 Works with GitHub or Azure Repos 
 Executes tasks automatically on code changes 
Steps to Create Azure Pipeline: 
Step 1: Create Project in Azure DevOps 
 Login to Azure DevOps 
 Click New Project 
 Enter project name 
 Select visibility (Public/Private) 
 Click Create 
Step 2: Import GitHub Repository 
 Go to Repos → Import Repository 
 Copy GitHub repository URL

 Paste and click Import 
Step 3: Create Pipeline 
 Go to Pipelines → Create Pipeline 
 Select repository (GitHub/Azure Repos) 
 Choose conﬁguration: 
o Example: Maven Project (Java Web App) 
 Select Azure subscription 
 Click Create 
Step 4: Select Web App Service 
 Choose existing Azure Web App 
 Click Validate and Conﬁgure 
 Azure automatically generates YAML ﬁle 
Step 5: Save and Run Pipeline 
 Click Save and Run 
 Pipeline starts execution 
3. Azure Pipeline Stages 
Pipeline mainly has two stages: 
1) Build Stage 
 Compile source code 
 Run tests 
 Package application (JAR/WAR) 
2) Deploy Stage 
 Deploy application to Azure Web App 
 Makes application live

Common Modiﬁcations 
1. Change project path

2. Change application name

3. Add testing step

goals: 'clean test package' 
4. Change deployment package 
package: '**/* .jar' 
5. Add multiple stages (Dev, Test, Prod) 
 Working of Azure Pipeline 
1. Developer commits code to GitHub 
2. Pipeline is triggered automatically 
3. Build stage compiles and tests code 
4. Artifact (WAR/JAR) is created 
5. Deploy stage uploads app to Azure 
6. Application runs on web server
